subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT AND CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION ACT AUTHORIZATION FOR CMHC TO MAKE INTEREST REDUCTION GRANTS, CASH GRANTS, ETC., TO ENCOURAGE HOUSE CONSTRUCTION

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, December 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Sharp (for the Minister of State for Urban Affairs) that Bill C-77, to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT AND CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION ACT AUTHORIZATION FOR CMHC TO MAKE INTEREST REDUCTION GRANTS, CASH GRANTS, ETC., TO ENCOURAGE HOUSE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak for very long, but I think it is necessary to point out that this legislation, like a lot of other legislation that is brought into the House, will not do much to solve the problem it is supposed to solve. I mentioned last night that we would have a much better housing system if we had originally established CMHC as an agency to build one class of house for those who cannot raise money in any other way. If over the years we had had a revolving fund, the payments made to CMHC would have been available to be reinvested. I am thinking about the system we follow with regard to the banks. We keep reserves in relation to the amount of lending which can take place somewhere in the range of one to eight: for every $1 deposited, the banks lend $8. It seems to me that this system could be followed with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation if we used the payments as a revolving fund rather than coming back to parliament every few months for a change in policy and a new direction.
Mr. Speaker, we are not building houses in Canada. We have a surplus of lumber and a surplus of building materials. There is a very high rate of unemployment in the construction industry. Despite this, a large number of Canadians are looking for houses that they can afford. Maybe Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should be buying land themselves. We should be establishing federal municipalities, if necessary, and constructing housing for Canadians.
I am always amazed at how quickly this government hides behind the constitution and the responsibility of the provinces. But when it came to the anti-inflation legislation, they did not bother about the constitution at all but decided the provinces could go along with them or stay out. They should be doing that with housing. We work out all kinds of arrangements with the provinces, and most citizens are not even aware that the federal government is involved; they think the schemes are provincial but are financed by the federal government through CMHC.
For some time, veterans' housing was separate. Recently, when the Veterans Land Act was ended, we were told that veterans would have special privileges under the national housing scheme. Only two veterans have taken advantage of the special arrangements, and approximately 50 have taken advantage of the AHOP program. The veterans obvi-
December 5, 1975

ously do not believe they are receiving preferential treatment from the national housing authority.
The government has participated with the provinces in a very cheap housing program-HOME. I should like to know where the inspectors of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are when it comes to maintaining the high standards of the corporation. I know of housing built under the program where you could not only look outside the house from inside, but from outside you could see inside without looking through the doors or windows. In my opinion, that kind of housing should be condemned. It does not meet any standard of construction; it cannot be heated properly and will not last very long.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation sets reasonable standards and if a contractor wants his house inspected it is done, but it is not easy for an individual who may have to wait as long as a month. Even banks have a great deal of trouble. I am always getting calls from them about their difficulties. In my area, however, I do not see any difficulty for the big contractors in getting inspectors to come in. They play footsy with each other. I can tell you of some terrible housing that is built and of disasters where large corporations are involved. Hedman is a good example. A major construction company in Timmins is building houses that should never be approved because they are unsafe in several respects.
There are many houses in Ottawa, where large corporations are involved, below the standards of Central Mortgage and Housing. In my opinion the head of Central Mortgage and Housing has built some houses that are dangerous and detrimental to the housing industry. Houses with aluminium wiring are potential death traps: in Ottawa, seven or eight fires have been directly attributed to it. I remember an instance last spring where the wiring was responsible for the death of a young girl. It should have been known that that type of wiring was causing considerable difficulty.
Central Mortgage and Housing is also approving trailers. One person I spoke to who lives in a trailer told me that you can feel along the wall and find it warm when the aluminium wiring gets hot. But people buying houses with aluminum wiring are not warned of the danger. I spoke to a government official who indicated that they had not been able to prove that aluminium wiring was unsatisfactory. When I asked if he would live in a house with aluminium wiring, he said, "Certainly not; it is dangerous." So it is not dangerous from a scientific point of view, and it is not dangerous according to the regulations the minister has put out, but it is dangerous for anyone who knows anything about it.
Housing standards are not enforced and in many cases we have agreed with the provinces to build substandard housing. My last point is that this minister is worse than any of the others we have had when it comes to changing the regulations and the subsidies for housing. In fact, only the real estate people can keep up to him. They are the only ones who can advise buyers and builders of all the advantages. Even the banks are having trouble in training their employees to understand the advantages of the current program, because it will be in effect only a few months before it is changed again. Any program that changes as often as the housing program cannot be good
National Housing Act
because most Canadians cannot take advantage of even the small advantages offered.
We are bribing the industry with subsidies. We are carrying on a policy of subsidizing the corporate bums, the large corporations that are building housing in this country. The result is that mostly expensive housing and shopping centres are being built because they bring greater returns. Other departments of governments are also to blame because the government ends up renting out accommodation that it cannot use. Mr. Speaker, Central Mortgage and Housing should not be providing assistance for building office space and shopping centres when in many cases there is a surplus of that kind of accommodation.
In parliament we are all aware that Parkinson's law is the guiding law of government. You build it, you create it, and you will use it. We have certainly done that in Ottawa and Hull with regard to office space. We have spent a great deal of money to provide unnecessary accommodation which obviously will have to be filled simply because it is there. This is lousy legislation, Mr. Speaker. The minister should sit down for a while instead of gadding about the country making speeches: he should look at some of the studies done in the past five or six years, none of which has been given any consideration, because every time a problem develops a new study is dreamed up.
There is a great need in this country for low-cost housing. If the minister considers the problem he will realize that to a large extent the banks subsidize the building of the low-cost housing that we need. If we are to meet our goals in housing we may have to control the banking industry, perhaps even nationalize it, to make sure that money is available for low-cost housing. That is where the need exists. The need is not so great in the case of middle-incomer earners. We need more housing for the poor and the banks must provide the money at low interest rates.
Finally, I suggest that when borrowers repay money to Central Mortgage and Housing the government should leave it there; in other words, the corporation should be empowered to lend again to other borrowers. This business of the government making available every so often a few hundred million dollars for housing is nothing but a gimmick. With every new program the ground rules are changed and people become confused. Would it not be better to let Central Mortgage and Housing retain repaid funds and lend them again? Instead of introducing new programs every so often, the government ought to embark on a long-range program of which people can be aware. Canadians should know today what will be available later in housing programs. The government ought to consider the Hellyer report and produce a white paper showing its long-range plans for housing.
The government must change its approach to housing. You cannot treat houses as you treat cars. People are being encouraged to buy cars before the end of the year because the Ontario government removed the sales tax on them until the year-end. They will reimpose it next year. Consequently, people are being pressured to buy cars. Buy now and save, they are told.
The minister tried to do much the same thing with housing. The house buyer who bought before a certain time
29956 -6614

December 5, 1975
National Housing Act
was to get a federal grant of $500. If he delayed buying, he would lose the grant. That is not the way to go about it. I suggest, therefore, that there is something wrong with the government's housing program. The government should explain to the average Canadian-not to the construction industry and not necessarily to the House of Commons- its housing program so that the average man will know which aspect of it will give him the greatest advantage. I think the government is obligated to do this.
If the minister is interested in solving the housing problems of our low-income people and is not merely interested in playing politics, he should work out a long-term program and explain it to the people. Since being appointed to his portfolio he has brought in three housing bills, not one of which, so far as I can see, has been worth supporting.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT AND CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION ACT AUTHORIZATION FOR CMHC TO MAKE INTEREST REDUCTION GRANTS, CASH GRANTS, ETC., TO ENCOURAGE HOUSE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Over the years, the government has been justifiably criticized for its so-called housing policy. As the Economic Council of Canada suggested, the government has treated housing policy as a sort of filler, in the same way as newspapers include fillers when their stories are shorter than anticipated. But this filler, this policy, has been used to stimulate the economy. As my colleague from Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) said, this program is nothing but shadow-boxing. It is a political program.
Of course people want a house of their own. Therefore, housing programs have always been political programs. I am not against political things except when they involve something as important as housing. In housing there must be a policy, and we have seen no policy. Of course, at election times housing policy becomes part of the government's program. It tells people what it will do to encourage home building and it says, "We will put money into such programs." And not only this government has said that. I do not say this government is exclusively to blame in that regard. However, it seems that the federal government's housing policy-and I include the policies of some provinces-has consisted of gimmickry rather than any attempt to come to grips with our needs. An adequate housing policy has not been established. The minister may say that this kind of gimmickry has been successful and that it has worked, although it has not always. That is hardly justification to those who are serious about solving the severe housing problem in Canada. When I speak of a severe housing problem, I do not mean that most Canadians are ill-housed or suffer from housing problems. Most Canadians do not suffer from housing problems and therein lies the great difficulty of determining what is a good housing program.
About two years ago I did a survey in my constituency. I asked my constituents, "Are you adequately housed or are you experiencing a housing problem?" About 90 per cent of the people replied that they were not experiencing any housing difficulties. One woman said, "Yes, I have a housing problem. His name is Richard." Nevertheless, a signifi-

cant group in this country is suffering from serious housing difficulties. The parliamentary secretary, who I presume delivered the speech on behalf of the minister, defined them as the ill, the poor and the elderly. I wish the people who write these marvellous speeches were responsible for implementing policy, because invariably we run into a non-sequitur. On the one hand we see definitions and an outline of what must be done, while on the other the proposals put forward in no way meet the need defined.
What will be the effect of the present proposal? This business of encouraging home ownership has increased the cost of every home in this country. Every time the government subsidizes people and allows them to acquire property, it makes more money available for bidding up the price of housing. We have seen this happen over and over again. The government has subsidized a small segment of the Canadian population but not that segment which is most in need.
Home owners have derived great capital advantage from the government's program which has forced up the price of houses. Presumably, that is one reason why it is so difficult to introduce an adequate housing policy in this country. Most people have a vested interest in seeing the price of houses rise. Most home owners look after their property, and although most say they deplore the sharp rise in house prices they are content to note how much their personal wealth has increased as a consequence of government programs. Certainly, that has been the effect of these programs.
You can see this sort of thing happening in other areas. For instance, consider government programs designed to encourage young people to buy farms. Every time we make credit easier we force up the price of farms. The same thing applies to housing. Every time the government introduces a program for encouraging people to buy housing, whether by giving a $500 federal grant on top of the $1,500 Ontario grant or any other method, the end result is that house prices rise. Is this what the government wants? Is this what the minister wants? If so, let him say so. That is one of the great consequences of what he is doing.
Let us discuss home ownership. There has been a terrible tendency to equate home ownership with living accommodation as though they are exactly the same. Obviously, home ownership and living accommodation have a relationship. One of the main reasons people buy homes is to have accommodation for themselves. What is often overlooked, or certainly is not stated, is that home ownership is more than just accommodation. Home ownership is a method of investment. What the government is doing is being very partial to a group of investors. That is what is really involved.
The government is creating two classes of citizens in this country, those who own and those who must rent accommodation. All the advantages are in favour of those who own. They are subsidized in the purchase of their home and in some cases are sustained in the payment of their mortgages. They receive benefits under the Income Tax Act, in contrast to those who have to rent. Is this the kind of society we want, where one group of people who are
December 5, 1975

fortunate to have surplus income and are able to save some money receive advantages on top of that?
The hon. member for Broadview documented the effect of some government programs such as registered retirement savings plans and things of that kind. We go beyond subsidizing and there is a tremendous amount of dissatisfaction engendered among those who do not receive any benefit. When the $500 grant came in I received many bitter complaints. People were asking if they were eligible for the grant with respect to houses they had bought two months earlier. I had to tell them they were not eligible unless they had purchased after a certain date.
How fair is a program that on an arbitrary basis, or depending on the political whims of the government, provides great capital benefit to some Canadians but not to others? The minister may say, in his defence, that we need to stimulate employment and this can be done by providing an increased housing stock, something that is badly needed. This has been said by various ministers over the years. Surely there are better ways of doing this than the subsidization programs the government now has.
It almost looks as though the Liberal party commissions the MacLaren Advertising Company to determine which group will have to be pleased in the next election. That company comes up with a target group. It may be young married swingers looking to do certain things. The company then tells the government what kind of program they must design in order to satisfy the target group. The poor are never a target group because they do not vote to the same extent as other people. So why bother pleasing them? They may have the greatest needs, but they are not as great a political force. Therefore, programs are not designed to please them. Programs are designed for the middle-class group. They please those who can be expected to be grateful to the government for bringing in measures of this type. They do not come to grips with the serious problems of the 5 per cent or 10 per cent of the population completely outside the housing market.
This minister has an opportunity of doing what others in that ministry have not done, that is, to deal with the housing problem in this country. For most people, the private housing market can take care of their needs. However, there is a group which the market can never take care of; therefore, their needs must be met. They cannot be adequately met by the gimmickry of a $500 bonus, the AHOP program or other forms of subsidization: if they do help, it is only at a marginal, accidental and incidental level.
We should look at the figures to see who really needs housing. Who is really in trouble with regard to housing? As the minister has said, it is the aged. We should be doing more with regard to housing for senior citizens. I should point out that our record in senior citizens' housing is not all that bad; it has been one of the finest programs on which this country has ever embarked. If you live in an area where the municipality has been farsighted enough to take advantage of the provisions for building senior citizens' housing, you will find senior citizens who are managing well on their old age pension. However, this is only because they have adequate housing at their disposal. Where there is good public housing available, in many cases senior citizens do better on retirement than they did
National Housing Act
during their working lives. Where that housing is not available, senior citizens just cannot manage. That has to be a top priority. We are so close to solving this problem that to relax with regard to it now would be criminal. That is one program that should be expanded.
In my own area of Waterloo-Cambridge there is a program that has been very successful. Frankly, without public housing I do not know where families with children would live. Who is in desperate need? Young people have no need. Single people do not have a housing problem unless they so choose. Young married couples in good health do not have a housing problem. They may have a problem of choice, but there is no real housing problem for them anywhere in Canada. Those who have a housing problem are those who have children. The problem is getting worse every year. A recent ruling by the province provides that if an apartment owner in the city of Toronto wants to exclude children and rent to adults only, that is fine. What happens in that situation?
You can understand older people who want peace and quiet, or swingers who do not want children getting in their way, having this self-centred attitude. But what about public responsibility? Where do people with children go? If you have three or four children you cannot find rental accommodation. If you have a lot of money you do not have to worry because you can purchase a home. However, for those with children who have to rent, without public housing they would end up on the street. This is one program that should be expanded. The minister may say that the budget has been increased slightly, but the evidence is otherwise.
The hon. member for Broadview documented the sharp decline in the percentage of aid being directed to public housing as against that being directed to other areas. I suggest we should get out of the AHOP program. In fact, the whole program of subsidizing ownership should be discarded in favour of providing the money for public housing. That is the serious problem. I agree that it is a little easier for people to buy housing with a subsidy, but what is desperately needed is housing for families with children. There is no sense in saying that they should not have had children; the children are here. This is not the time to moralize or to say they should not have done it; the children are here and have to be looked after.
There are many advantages to public housing. It does not have to be bad. I can tell the minister that public housing in my area is good. It is some of the best housing in my area. I am delighted to say that. I know it is not always like that, because some public housing should never have been built. The public housing in my area was planned intelligently. It was done years ago. We did not have to deal with neighbourhood groups who seem to have a vested interest against public housing. I have in mind groups who want to be protected against the sight of children, or perhaps against the sight of the poor. In fact, they are probably one of the most reactionary elements in our society, all in the name of neighbourhood control and participatory democracy. They are the ones I used to fight years ago because I tried to build a sidewalk and they would not let us go through their nice lawns.

December 5, 1975
National Housing Act
That question aside, the point is the government has some measure of control. The government says that is up to the municipality, it is up to the province. Admittedly, they are the ones who have to make the final decisions on zoning, and so on. But the government has a great deal of clout with the mortgage money at its disposal, with the assistance it is prepared to offer municipalities. The government can say that unless municipalities pursue intelligent policies like making provision for families with children, there will be no money going into the area. This is a tough stand to take, but the government has a responsibility, particularly since it is involved in things like immigration and mobility problems. They say, "All right; we have an immigration policy, but what happens to an immigrant once he hits the city is of no concern to us." There isn't any housing, or he tries to compete with those who have been there a long time and all kinds of ill will develop because there is a shortage of housing. It is said that if competition exists, that is not our responsibility but a municipal responsibility.
If we have a mobility program that moves people from the coast to central Canada, it is said that is not our problem: once we provide a mobility grant, it is no concern of ours. You cannot have these federal programs, you cannot have an immigration policy or a mobility policy without at the same time making provision to house the people affected by those policies. That is why these policies fail. It is because we don't make these provisions. There was a time, a couple of years ago-there aren't any jobs now, anyway-when there was a lot of work in Toronto, a lot of work in northern Ontario and other parts of Canada, and people were trying to encourage migration from high unemployment areas to low unemployment areas. But people weren't moving, and the reason they were not moving was that they had nowhere to live when they moved. This is what a housing policy should really be trying to deal with.
I do not understand the government's mathematics in saying we are trying to encourage the private developer, or we are going to provide some assistance or some encouragement for professionals to invest in apartment construction in order to get more construction, as though that doesn't cost money. I presume the government would say, "We do not have the funds," or, "We cannot raise the funds." But that is really a camouflage. It is coming out of the public treasury when you subsidize somebody or allow them to write off their losses on one activity against their income from another. That is just as direct a cost to the government and Canadian taxpayers as it is to go out and raise the funds directly and charge them the tax they should have been paying.
We went through this business with the white paper. One of the provisions of the white paper on taxation, one of the progressive things it did and one of the things it corrected in our tax system, was that it prevented people writing off the losses of one apartment building against the profits of another. People have accumulated millions of dollars in capital assets because they have never paid a cent in taxes by using this route. We got rid of that measure only to have it come in the back door now. The government is acknowledging its own failure by saying,

"The builders were right when they told us, if you close this tax loophole you will not get the construction we were giving you before." So the government has backed away from its position in the white paper, something it never should have done, and it is now allowing this other method for investors to get into the business.
You do not need that kind of private investor when you are dealing with the kind of problems I have outlined, the problems of the old and those of the families. When the great socialist millenium comes, perhaps we will have housing as a public utility: we will have the right to housing, the right to accommodation accepted in the same way as we accept the right to medical attention, to hospital services and to the old age pension. But we are some distance away from that. Therefore, like many other things we have to deal with the most urgent problem, and the most urgent of our problems is public housing for families with children. If we do not do this, I just don't know where they are going to find rental accommodation or housing. That has to be the target area of any government proposal. For most Canadians the minister can take his euphoric position that we are one of the best housed people in the world. That is true for most Canadians. But for some Canadians it is shocking and shameful that these policies are directed toward providing benefits for the middle classes and to those who are already reasonably well off, rather than dealing directly with the problems of the poor.
If the minister is really interested in helping the poor- and I think he is-another area he has to explore, if he does not want these subsidies, if he does not want public housing, if he wants to do it some other way, is to provide more income to people with housing needs, people with family responsibilities and obligations whose talents, skills or vocational positions do not permit them to obtain adequate housing. That can be done through family allowances. We could have a housing grant go out through the family allowance program, providing a sum of money to assist people go into the private market in order to buy houses, because that is where the problem is.
If the minister doesn't want to go one route of providing more public housing, then surely he has to admit the failure of his program to help the poor and advise his cabinet colleagues to do something with the family allowance scheme or some income supplement scheme. Otherwise, no one can really commend either his work or the work of his predecessors in doing anything about housing. We are so close to coming up with an intelligent housing policy-we have solved so many problems in this country-that to stop short at this time and play political games with housing, gimmick after gimmick, depending on the political whims of the time, is really unforgiveable.
I want to return to something I started to say earlier. Housing or home ownership is more than accommodation; it is a form of investment. When the minister says that no one should have to pay 25 per cent of their income for accommodation, I don't think he is correct. Private home ownership for people, unless they have children-I am talking about people who do not have families-is an investment choice, it is not just a housing choice. If all they want is housing, there is a great deal of housing and good rental accommodation around. But they have decided they do not want to go that route. They want to be a home
December 5, 1975

owner. Then they are investing and they have to be considered as investors. They should not be supplemented. The government does all kinds of things to help investors in this country; but is it correct, when you have severe housing problems for some of our people, to go around augmenting the wealth of those who are already reasonably well off? This is really the effect of many of these programs.
The minister may want to take a few minutes at this point to reply to some of the things that have been said in the debate; therefore I shall conclude, but not because I have said everything I wanted to say. There is one thing I want the minister to look at because I consider him to be an intelligent and sensitive man; I should like him to look at the kind of mess he has inherited and is perpetuating.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the closing minutes of the debate-because I think the matter should proceed now-I wish to say something to the minister concerning two matters which I consider to be important. The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) mentioned that housing is an investment and that it is wrong for the government to subsidize this kind of thing. I think there is some merit in that argument.
I hope the minister will consider that in order to make housing less attractive as an investment and more attractive regarding what it is intended to be, a roof over one's head and over one's family, there is a duty on all governments-not just this government but provincial and municipal governments-to ensure there is a greater supply of serviced land. This shortage is creating to a great degree the conditions about which the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge is concerned and which concern us all, not only in this House of Commons but in the country, who are home owners and who look at the acceleration of the price of property and realize that in terms of housing the acceleration of value has been unconscionable. I suggest that the importance of a program with regard to serviced land and its availability cannot be over emphasized.
One other matter I should like the minister to consider, as we look at this question as an ongoing consideration in this country, is the dreadful tendency in Canada to live in our large cities. There is a new concept in the legislation. There is a certain viability and a certain quality of life available in the smaller communities, and I hope the minister will use the powers he has, limited as they are in the constitutional sense but large in the moral sense, to encourage housing development around existing smaller towns. I think this is important not only for the provision of housing but, as well, for the social fabric of our community. I think we have forgotten about this in Canada. There is still time in our country, but that time is running short having regard to the projection of statistics.
I just wished to bring those two matters to the attention of the government. We are not just building boxes for people to live in, but we are playing with the social fabric of our country. The minister's program today, his programs of the future and the programs of future governments must be looked at from the point of view of their social attributes as well as the provision of four walls and a roof.

Mr. Speaker, first I should all like to apologize for not having been in the House when this debate commenced. I am grateful to my parliamentary secretary who spoke on my behalf. I have been following the transcripts of the debate and the contributions of various members. I am especially grateful to those hon. members. I made arrangements for the parliamentary secretary to speak on my behalf only after speaking to the leaders of the opposition parties and the spokesmen, in this area, for those parties. They understood the necessity and the urgency of my being away and they supported me on this very important subject. It is important, I think, nationally and internationally in relation to the United Nations Conference on Human Settlements to be held in Vancouver next year.
I appreciate the support of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) in this regard. I might say I have been encouraged by my visit to Vancouver and the response by the city council there and the community at large. As hon. members know, we are going ahead with the conference. It will be highly successful for Canada and for the United Nations.
I was especially interested in the two speeches I had the opportunity to hear today dealing with housing and, in a specific sense, also the philosophy. There is an understanding that we do not have a crisis in the sense that we are a badly housed nation, but there are aspects of housing which are quite critical. Housing has been considered much more than a place to live in, in many cases. There was also mention of the urgency concerning the acquisition of serviced land. I was very grateful to my friend, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), for his appreciation of such development in southeastern part of the city. In respect of the Lebreton development, the land assembly work is already done and we are moving ahead in a very comprehensive way, as is the case in the southeastern part of the city. I realize how important this is to the hon. member's constituency.
I believe my parliamentary secretary explained the urgency of dealing with this legislation as quickly as may be allowed. It is important legislation. I am sure all members of the House realize how important it is. I should like to deal in a general way with some of the observations made by hon. members opposite and emphasize some of the important features. I note that some hon. members recalled statements my parliamentary secretary and I have made regarding some of the most serious housing problems in Canada, as well as the number of families inadequately housed in crowded or unsanitary facilities.
I see it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I shall continue after lunch.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we adjourned for lunch I was referring to the comments of hon. members in this debate relating to the number of families which are inadequately housed, live in crowded conditions or lack sanitary facilities. This is a matter of concern to me. I am glad these figures are receiving attention and being remembered, because I believe they should be uppermost in everyone's mind when considering the housing needs of this country. My parliamentary secretary began this debate by saying, on my behalf and on behalf of the government, that these people's needs are the number one priority. Indeed, these figures are always uppermost in my mind.
As the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge said, we are the best housed people in the world and we do not have a housing crisis per se. However, as I said in my remarks before lunch, there are many critical areas in housing and I carry in my pocket a list of statistics relating to housing because that is the challenge we face and that is where we begin. It is a rather strange phenomenon that each time the government introduces a new housing initiative, many hon. members react as if all previous housing programs had been superseded or wiped out. Because we are improving and expanding the Assisted Home Ownership Program, for instance, to help more people and to reach down more deeply into the lower income levels, that does not mean we have gone out of the public housing business or that we have abandoned our non-profit and co-operative housing programs. We invested more than $600 million in these programs in 1975, programs directed at least at the most urgent housing problems, almost one-third of the total CMHC capital budget of $1.6 billion. I have undertaken that the funding for these programs will be substantially increased in 1976.
When we say that social housing is our first priority, we back up our conviction with more dollars. It is precisely by utilizing and directing private lenders into the markets which are also of concern to many Canadians that we free more dollars for the lower income groups, for public housing, for non-profit housing, for senior citizens' housing and for rural and native housing. These are the programs which will have additional funding because the private sector will be looking at the market which does not require the same degree of public support.
As is apparent from the trend in this debate, there seems be to general agreement about the nature of the problems we face; the need to increase the supply of housing, particularly low and moderately-priced housing, the need to reduce the high cost of land and the cost of financing. There is not very much disagreement with the action we propose to take. The common cry-which I have heard before-is, "You will never make it work". Let me assure the House that we will make it work, and we are making it work.

speechtext:
I do not lie down and die easily because they say some nasty words, are skeptical or do not have the same faith in Canadians that I have. There might be times we do not achieve our target. That does not disturb me very much. I know we have done the best we can. We agreed that we must increase the supply of housing in Canada, and we say we will build a minimum of one million new homes in the next four years. To do that we must emphasize, at least for the time being, new construction to build up the existing stocks. To do that we must increase the supply of serviced land, as the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton indicated. We will accomplish this objective by making residential development much more attractive to the municipalities. We already give them favourable land assembly terms. We will give them money for water treatment and mains and $1,000 for every low-cost, medium-density unit that they approve and build. I think this is an aggressive attack on the problem of land supply.
I have had some very good discussions, also, with my provincial colleagues about the problems arising from municipal approval processes and zoning. There has been a very useful exchange of ideas, expecially at our last meeting of provincial ministers. But this is a subject which is constantly on their minds and is a concern which we share with them. Although the matter clearly lies within provincial jurisdiction, it is a serious enough problem that it has national implications. I share the concern of the provincial ministers and that concern is reflected in some of the measures we are proposing now, from which they can take off and move further in their own jurisdictions.
To meet our targets we will need another $750 million in private money in addition to the approximately $7 billion which private investors put up this year. Some hon. members say that is not enough. They say that will give us only
20,000	or 25,000 new starts in 1976, and that is right. That would bring our 1976 starts up to about 235,000, and that is our target. It is consistent with our goal of one million good quality, well designed housing starts by 1980. How many would they like-two million, three million? Our target is realistic and related to population growth and household formations. I think our track record is pretty good in that field. It also takes into consideration the real delivery capacity of the industry.
Last year I said that 210,000 would be a realistic target for 1975, and now, in spite of all the skepticism which I just mentioned, we are going to make it. When I speak of one million starts with an emphasis on the lower price ranges, this target will be achieved without sacrificing quality. In that connection I should like to advise the House that on December 17 we are convening a meeting of provincial officials, consumers, builders and lenders in a
December 5, 1975

determined effort to move forward on consumer warranties. At the last federal-provincial meeting on housing there was substantial provincial support for a national system administered by an independent council, and I am hopeful we can quickly resolve any remaining obstacles.
When we say we will have more private investment, the reply always is that the lenders will not come through, that they will cross us up somewhere along the line. Some hon. members suggest that we pass a law telling the lenders where they have to invest their money. That is one way. We could do it that way. But I have spoken with some of the lenders and I do not think we will have any problem at all. As a matter of fact, I am confident we will not have any problem. After all, we are not asking them to pour their money down the drain. They are persuaded that this kind of shift in priorities will not only be socially useful but will be a sensible decision as well. Even without that specific direction, just by offering programs they started to see the value of those as business decisions in the latter part of this year. It did not really catch hold until about July. I urged hon. members then, and I urge them now, to assist the passage of this legislation through the House because there are time lags and it does take time to catch up. Every week or month of delay holds up the implementation of this program.
We are agreed that mortgate rates are too high, and this House has just passed some very important and significant legislation which supports a vigorous attack on the root causes of high interest rates. One hon. member suggested that I could solve the problem of high interest rates by announcing to the financial institutions that interest rates shall be 8 per cent. I can assure the hon. member that if it were that easy, I would not hesitate for a minute. I might be tempted to say that interest rates shall be 6 per cent. Why not? The fact is that most lenders operate on a margin of 1 !4 per cent to 2 per cent between what they borrow for and what they lend at. Not many people would be prepared to accept 4>/2 per cent cent interest on their bank accounts to make 6 per cent mortgages possible.
As long as financial institutions must pay 10 per cent to attract term deposits, I do not think we can be expected to compel them by law to lend funds at a lower rate than they borrow for and, on top of that, to absorb their administrative costs. I would not expect workers to have their pensions lowered and to invest their money on a return which did not at least reflect the realities of the economic scene today. They cannot be expected to do that, and they would not do it. In the meantime, we are offering help with mortgage payments to people who need it most. For people with families and low or moderate incomes we are increasing the government's outright grants to help them buy their homes without putting out more than 25 per cent of their income in monthly payments. For people who are without children or who are not so hard up, we are offering some temporary help until they get established, a loan effectively to reduce their interest rate to 8 per cent, which must be paid back eventually but which is interest free for the first five years. That is pretty fair. We are helping people get established. We are helping young families get into the market, and when they pay the money back they are paying it to their fellow taxpayers, their fellow citizens. They have an obligation to pay it back, but at no time
National Housing Act
are we asking them to pay out more than 25 per cent of their income.
One hon. member said we are offering some people easy credit and leading them into unmanageable debt. That is not so. Borrowers will have to discuss their financial arrangements with the lenders and will have to conform to NHA loan regulations. We believe that when people know what they are getting into, they will make the right and responsible decision. We have much faith in the common sense of ordinary Canadians. Perhaps that is why they support us.
We are going to make similar arrangements with people who will agree to build good rental accommodation at reasonable cost. In return for government help, they have to sign an agreement with us about rent and other matters such as maintenance standards, and so on. When we talk about critical areas, I consider that the whole area of rental is one of the critical areas. As the hon. member for Water-loo-Cambridge said, housing is not always a matter of ownership, it is a matter of accommodation and rental as well. For some people rental is the best solution, and it is a solution which is being exacerbated by our inflationary spiral and by some of the restrictions of which the hon. member spoke today.
Some hon. members say that AHOP price limits are too low in many places. That may be so. We are constantly reviewing these prices in relation to the market and I will have an announcement to make in that regard within a few days. However, it is surprising what builders can do when they have to. We can make them work to come up with a good, well designed and comfortable home within AHOP terms. We aim to have some influence on keeping prices down instead of just following every rise in the market. When I first came into this job, people said they could not buy houses at those prices, and they were right. The builders said they could not build them at those prices, and they were wrong. When we were the only action in town, the only place mortgage money was available, the builders found they could build very good houses for that money.
In some parts of the country the AHOP limits will allow a single-family detached house; in some places it will be a townhouse or a condominium. None of these options is a terrible hardship, especially if people who otherwise could not make it are allowed to get into the home ownership market. They are given security of tenure which they otherwise would not have, and they are allowed to begin to build an equity in some property. Very few of these families would expect to spend their lives in their first home.
Some hon. members have suggested that the federal housing action program will be inflationary. On this point I firmly disagree. It is essentially aimed at increasing the supply of affordable housing. That is what AHOP and assisted rental programs do. They are decreasing the pressures on the market with respect to the cost of housing, which in terms of ownership is perhaps the largest single payment or obligation any family assumes in its lifetime. For those masses of people who have to rent in Canada, with the vacancy rate as it is the pressures are on for rents to go up because they are not economic these days. They have not risen as high as the cost of replacement. We are trying to make it possible, and that is deflationary.

National Housing Act
At the same time, by requiring purchasers of expensive housing to make bigger down payments we are cooling out demand in the high-priced ranges and increasing the supply of capital for the kind of housing we need in this country. This will cool out the existing housing market, but that is not so bad. If we have a home which we want to sell-and perhaps we will get less for it next year; I hope that is the case,-because we want to move somewhere else, we will be able to buy less expensively because, as one hon. member said, some prices have risen unconscionably and we intend to cool that market out. These are speculative gains. We have said this is the type of housing people are living on, rather than living in. It became one of the hedges against inflation and I think that situation will be reversed, not dramatically and not immediately but we will see a gradual cooling off. Indeed, in many places that has started to occur.
To wind up these brief remarks, I appreciate the contributions which have been made in this debate by hon. members on all sides of the House. I think all those who have spoken have helped in some way to illuminate the real challenges which we face in ensuring that all Canadians, not just most Canadians, are well housed. I commend the principles of this legislation to the serious consideration of all hon. members and I look forward to a more detailed consideration of its provisions at the committee stage. Indeed, I am prepared to sit morning, noon and night seven days a week, if necessary, in the hope that all manner of questions will be addressed to me and properly answered, and the legislation thoroughly dealt with so that we can give it third reading before we recess for the Christmas holidays.

Like so many undertakings of succeeding governments in Canada, the purpose has not in every case fulfilled this expectation. I am therefore sorry to say there is a fair amount of cynicism about the purpose of the department, in my part of Canada at least.
Some years ago it was the "in" thing to say that all the problems of the department would be solved if there could be decentralization. Instead of expediting the decisions of this department, I think it is reasonable to say that in many cases another layer of bureaucracy has interrupted the flow of information and decision-making between the federal government and the provincial governments. This is not a harsh criticism. It is, though, a comment on the fact that often the best plans, made with the best will in the world, do not work out in the best interests of the program.
I have two constituency concerns, Mr. Speaker. Regional Development Incentives Act

What benefits has the program brought to those special areas designated under the legislation? speechtext:
It annoys me, Mr. Speaker, to note so much criticism in our newspapers, on television and radio, of a good program. We must have critics because we want to live in a free democracy, but let them get their facts correct and mention the good with the bad.
I can say now that if the Department of Regional Economic Expansion had not been established by a Liberal government, the slow growth areas of this country would have been in a far worse condition today. Their condition would have been terrible. At the end of December this year, the designation of the special area encompassing Arnprior, Renfrew, Pembroke, Barry's Bay and Bancroft will end, after extensions by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I plead with the government to extend the designation for another 12 months. I plead for the people in the northern part of my riding, in the district of Nipissing, to be included uner the Regional Incentives Development Act (RIDA).
My reasons are these. Two days ago I received a call from a major industry in the area which had been established under DREE, it has been a good corporate citizen but was forced to lay off 60 employees because its furniture component sales to the United States dropped almost to nothing. The firm established in an area which was almost down and out and put about 300 people on its payroll. I have been in touch with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and DREE, and have tried my utmost to save the entire complex. Mr. Speaker, the

December 5, 1975
Regional Development Incentives Act entire population of Mattawa, consisting of about 3,000 people, and all the people who live on small farms near the town, will be in great jeopardy if this industry disappears. The three branches of this furniture business constitute the only industry operating in that section of the upper Ottawa Valley. It is for this reason that I am supporting the bill before us and asking that this area be taken, not just into serious consideration but realistic consideration when the time comes for renewal of the program in 1976.
I could list other statistics for the county of Renfrew and city of Pembroke but I shall not do so at this time because other members want to speak on this bill. However, I sincerely request that the area I have mentioned be reinstated for another 12 months. At the present time, the city of Pembroke and the county of Renfrew are negotiating with the provincial government of Ontario for a General Development Agreement. This has been going on for months but the agreement has not been signed. I should amend that by saying subagreement, because the general agreement covers the entire province.
I know that many members of this House look upon the province of Ontario as the rich brother of this nation. That may be true for certain areas of the province, but the Ottawa Valley, on both sides of the river, is quite often compared with the conditions existing in the maritime provinces. In fact, many members of the Canadian armed forces who retire from the service at CFB Petawawa remain in the Ottawa Valley because it is so similar to their home province in the maritimes. There is a very close relationship here.
While there are rapid growth areas in certain parts of Ontario, many areas of this province are very similar to the slow growth regions of Canada. Because they are slow growth regions, many municipalities, counties and districts cannot afford the water and sewage services about which the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweath-er) just spoke. Therefore, they do not have the up to date industrial parks, with all the facilities, to offer incoming industries in the same way as the rapid growth areas of Ontario.
The local municipalities make suggestions as to what they feel should be included in the General Development subagreements which is a federal-provincial program. Those GDA subagreements should include water and sewage services in order to upgrade industrial parks. However, even if an area 250 or 350 miles from a large urban area has an up to date industrial park, industry still locates in the large centres of this country. What we need in rural Ontario, and in the small municipalities across this province which do not have the same benefits as the large urban areas because the latter have a greater municipal tax base, is an incentive program built into the GDA program. This is necessary if it is going to work effectively and efficiently for those areas.
The GDA subagreements should cut away some of the red tape. Unfortunately, this is common with many federal-provincial agreements. It is very important that we have a good working relationship among officials at the federal and provincial levels. It is important that there be close conversations between the federal and provincial govern-

ments on a very sincere basis. We should not stall in those areas classified as slow growth. There should be sewage and water facilities in industrial park areas. Assistance should be given to municipalities so that they can provide better sewage disposal plants, upgraded water facilities, sewer lines, water lines, and so on. Much of this has already been done by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and for that I compliment that Crown corporation: they have done a tremendous job at that level.
In order to provide for the growth that will take place as a result of the development of upgraded industrial parks, we must also provide facilities for those who will be moving into these areas. The increased population will increase the necessity for facilities. This will drain off some of the large populations needlessly concentrated in certain areas of Canada, creating added expense by more expensive housing, for example.
Many people have moved from rural areas into large urban areas. Others who have lived in urban areas all their lives see a certain value to the small town or small city way of life. It offers them a rural landscape, natureland in the shield area, as it is known in eastern Ontario. Not only does this increase the quality of life for people, but through this legislation we are discussing, it provides for their livelihood. It will slow the growth in the large urban centres of Ontario which, if allowed to grow at the present rate, would cost this country a fortune. Do we in Canada want a New York City, Chicago or Detroit?
Under the legislation that we are discussing, and under the General Development subagreements at the federal-provincial level, there should be programs to develop small communities across Canada and to provide for a better quality of life for our people.
I want to say that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), who by the way is my seatmate, certainly has my total support in his endeavours as far as the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is concerned. I hope these programs will continue to go forward in the years to come so that we do not get into the problems I discussed a few minutes ago.
In closing, I should like to reiterate the request I put on record earlier with regard to a 12-month extension of the special area in Renfrew county. I should like to see more rapid progress in signing the sub-CDA agreement between the two senior levels of government concerning my area of the Ottawa Valley. I should like to say of the Ottawa Valley in general that the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Lefebvre) who has worked very closely with me over the years-and we have an excellent rapport-faces many of the same problems and we both support the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to the hilt. Once again I pay tribute to the people of that department regardless of the criticism which has been thrust at them from time to time.
I should also like to add that I am prepared at any time to put the plus factors together and stack them up against the minus factors as a whole in the Ottawa Valley as far as the effect the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has had on our locale.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND CERTAIN PROVISIONS TO DECEMBER 31, 1981
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make two or three points in connection with DREE. I am not sure everyone will agree with me with regard to some of it, but I think I should emphasize that I am speaking in a very personal sense. I want to make it clear that I am not expressing a point of view on behalf of my party. There are certain views I hold in connection with DREE which I feel I can express at this stage of my political career without any misunderstanding. These are things I have said before and I would like to emphasize them again. I am sure there will be a good many on both sides of the House who will disagree with me. Nevertheless, it is important that some of these issues be discussed.
The first point I wish to make is this. It has been said many times that an attack on regional disparity involves, if it is to be effective, a very high degree of co-ordination within the government. It is so obvious I do not need to deal with the proposition at any length. It is evident that DREE could make a great effort to stimulate the economy of a region and that this effort could readily be offset by some countervailing policy adopted, perhaps unwittingly, by another department of the federal government.
The obvious example of this was when DREE was going ahead full force in 1969-1970 and when the Department of Finance was at the same time pursuing a policy of tight money-a tight fiscal policy. Those effects were felt first and foremost in areas of slower growth. Such a policy, pursued by the Department of Finance, negated the efforts of DREE. Then, again, there was the failure of the Department of Transport, for example, to pursue policies which complemented and reinforced the efforts made by DREE. This is another obvious instance where the thing could come apart and where a substantial effort made by the department could fall to the ground.
Also, there must, of course, be effective collaboration between the federal government and the province or provinces involved in particular programs. While there have been agreements between the federal government and particular provinces covering the development of certain parts of a province, I would say, speaking particularly of the Atlantic provinces, that there has not been the degree of co-operation or agreement essential as a foundation of an attack on regional disparity. I think, for example, of the long delay before the federal government and the province of Nova Scotia could come together to establish the so-called Magi experiment in the Halifax metropolitan area. This was a program which was announced by the federal government before the election of 1972. It drifted on for two or three years at least, substantially because the federal government and the government of Nova Scotia could not agree who would assume final responsibility for direction.
This is a key question with regard to regional development, and I do not pretend to have the complete answer: how would one secure within the federal government the necessary degree of co-ordination to launch an effective attack on regional disparity? Nor am I sure what kind of institutional arrangement might be needed within the federal government. I know some machinery has been established; I am sure there are interdepartmental committees, and so forth. But if the government is to make any dent in
Regional Development Incentives Act regional disparity in the Atlantic region, for example, during the next five years there has somehow to be a much higher degree of co-ordination of effort within the federal government itself and between the federal government and the provinces concerned. I am not sure, as I say, what the framework of the institutional arrangement should be, but I do say it does not exist today. There has not been, since DREE was launched, the necessary coordination and collaboration required for a successful effort.
It was rather naively assumed at the time the Department of Regional Economic Development was established that this department would in itself provide the necessary co-ordination of effort within the federal government. I think it was rather naively assumed that bringing together the agencies and what not that were brought together when DREE was established would in itself provide that necessary degree of co-ordination of federal effort. That obviously has not been the case.
I want to make it very clear, that to me it is not adequate for the federal government at this time simply to extend the life of DREE for a further period of five years and carry on with the same kind of inadequate institutional arrangements to do battle against regional disparity in an ineffective way. I want to make that point as forcefully as I can.
The second point I want to make, and this is where I expect I will run into specific disagreement from all quarters of the House, is that I think it is wrong and a substantial mistake to have anything like a uniform approach to regional economic development across the country. Let me make it clear what I mean. I think regional development in the Atlantic provinces, including parts of Quebec like the Gaspe Peninsula, have regional disparity problems that are different from those that exist generally in other parts of the country.
It would seem to me that what the Government of Canada should be concerned about basically is having vigorous regional economies in all parts of the country, in British Columbia, on the prairies, in the north, in Ontario and Quebec, and in the Atlantic provinces.
For example, I do not think the federal government should feel itself primarily responsible for assuring that all the communities in the Atlantic provinces are prosperous and dynamic. The federal government should not feel it has a primary responsibility to see that all the communities in my own province of Nova Scotia are dynamic in their growth. The responsibility of the federal government in connection with the Atlantic provinces is in terms of achieving a vigorous economy in the region which will develop its own dynamism.
One of the mistakes the federal government has made, and one of the things that is wrong with what the government has done to date, is that it is trying to do too much. What is wrong with the DREE program, in my judgment, is that the federal government is just trying to do too much rather than concentrate upon regional development, not allowing itself to be distracted, as I might put it, by thinking in terms of community development.
For example, with regard to the prairie provinces, and members from the prairie provinces might think this is a

December 5, 1975
Regional Development Incentives Act
purely gratuitous thing for me to say, I would think that the responsibility of the government in respect of the economy of that area is to help ensure, in co-operation with the governments of those provinces, a vigorous and diversified economy. As I understand it, one of the things the people living on the prairies want to see there is economic diversity.
To be blunt about it, I do not think the federal government should feel it is primarily concerned with the state of prosperity or otherwise of a particular community in Saskatchewan, Manitoba or Alberta. Of course there could be crises and catastrophes in respect of which the federal government would be expected to play its part.
It is my belief that in attempting to reach down below the region, assuming responsibility in terms of community development, the federal government through DREE is taking on so much it is not doing an adequate job and not concentrating itself adequately on the development of the region.
I am not suggesting that in a province like Ontario, for example, DREE should keep out all together. I can recognize that in terms of northern Ontario there is a region of sufficient size with enough in common that there is a problem of regional development. On the prairies a similar area may be that mid-north strip across the prairies and into British Columbia. There may be a problem there. I recognize that the Department of Regional Development should think in terms of regional development in these areas, but not in terms of uniform development within regions, which is more the responsibility of the provinces concerned.
If the Government of Canada adopts that approach then the programs it pursues and the methods it follows might well be very different in the Atlantic provinces and in eastern Quebec from those in northern Ontario or in western Canada. Such an approach might be very different, and the government might be much more effective and run much less risk of the federal agencies and departments involved being so bogged down in detail they cannot get anywhere really with regard to regional stimulus.
After all these years of DREE being in existence I have to say that there is no plan for the development of the Atlantic region as a whole. The Atlantic Provinces Advisory Committee, which succeeded the Atlantic Provinces Development Board, under the chairmanship of Professor Smith, emphasized time and time again a few years ago the importance of the federal government and the four provinces down there agreeing on a plan or a general approach. This has never been done. I do not know whether it has not been done because there has not been a will to achieve it, or because nobody has been able to produce a plan that looks as if it might work. Whatever the reason, there has been no plan put forward or adopted for that region as a whole, although there have been agreements entered into between the federal government and these provinces relating to parts of the provinces. The whole of Prince Edward Island is under a plan agreed to by Prince Edward Island and the Government of Canada, but that falls very far short of economic planning for the development of the maritime provinces or Atlantic region.
Are we going to enter the next five years in the life of DREE, drifting along as far as the Atlantic provinces are 
concerned the way we have been doing? I am not suggesting the people of the Atlantic provinces do not appreciate the effort that has been made, or the money that has been spent by the people of other parts of Canada in an attempt to attack the long standing and deep seated economic problems of the Atlantic region.
I ask whether the government is to drift into this renewal for another five years, going along in the same way as in recent years, simply improvising and certainly failing to produce any coherent attack on the problems of the Atlantic region? I am afraid that is exactly what is happening and that, as a result of this happening and continuing, the whole concept of fighting regional economic disparity in areas like the Atlantic provinces will become discredited. I am concerned that people in other parts of Canada will more and more become impatient about having to foot the bill. So I say to my colleagues in the House of Commons this afternoon that we are not doing very much simply in extending the life of DREE for another five years.
I say that members of the government and this House should face up to the inadequacy of what is being done. They should abandon the approach of having one uniform economic attack across the country. We should think in terms of our responsibility here being a regional one rather than thinking in terms of being responsible for the equal development of communities within regions, certainly in areas like the Atlantic provinces.
We should face up to the necessity of developing a coherent attack that is likely to produce some results rather than the kind of improvisation that is going on which has been very useful to particular communities but which has done very little indeed, I must say, to reduce economic disparity for the people in those regions as compared to people in other parts of the country.
I certainly intend to support the bill, Mr. Speaker. I will support the renewal of DREE's mandate, but I feel very strongly, when DREE is being given a mandate for another five years, that this is an appropriate time for the government to re-think the working of the DREE program, to re-think its approach, and to recognize that really at the present time it has not achieved a satisfactory program of regional development in the various parts of the country. The government must face up to the necessity of doing this. It will be a great tragedy if members of this House think they are doing their duty this afternoon simply by extending the life of DREE without at the same time facing up to the fact that DREE has been a very limited success despite the amount of money spent, and despite the good will behind it.
If members of this parliament are to discharge their responsibility to the people of Canada as a whole, as well as to the people living in these disadvantaged areas, I think they should make up their minds to face up to the responsibility and the challenge that a really effective fight against regional disparity involves. There must be co-ordination which DREE in itself does not provide. There must be a determined and orderly attack on these problems which is flexible in respect of the country as a whole.
December 5, 1975
